passage_1.text:
Many human phenomena and characteristics – such as behaviors, beliefs, economies, genes, incomes, life expectancies, and other things - are influenced both by geographic factors and by non-geographic factors. Geographic factors mean physical and biological factors tied to geographic location, including climate, the distributions of wild plant and animal species, soils, and topography. Non-geographic factors include those factors subsumed under the term culture, other factors subsumed under the term history, and decisions by individual people.

The differences between the current economies of North and South Korea cannot be attributed to the modest environmental differences between them. They are instead due entirely to the different government policies. At the opposite extreme, the Inuit and other traditional peoples living north of the Arctic Circle developed warm fur clothes but no agriculture, while equatorial lowland peoples around the world never developed warm fur clothes but often did develop agriculture. The explanation is straightforwardly geographic, rather than a cultural or historical quirk unrelated to geography. Aboriginal Australia remained the sole continent occupied only by hunter/gatherers and with no indigenous farming or herding. The explanation is biogeographic: the Australian continent has no domesticable native animal species and few domesticable native plant species. Instead, the crops and domestic animals that now make Australia a food and wool exporter are all non-native (mainly Eurasian) species such as sheep, wheat, and grapes, brought to Australia by overseas colonists.

Today, no scholar would be silly enough to deny that culture, history, and individual choices play a big role in many human phenomena. Scholars don't react to cultural, historical, and individual-agent explanations by denouncing "cultural determinism," "historical determinism,” or “individual determinism," and then thinking no further. But many scholars do react to any explanation invoking some geographic role, by denouncing "geographic determinism".

Several reasons may underlie this widespread but nonsensical view. One reason is that some geographic explanations advanced a century ago were racist, thereby causing all geographic explanations to become tainted by racist associations in the minds of many scholars other than geographers. But many genetic, historical, psychological, and anthropological explanations advanced a century ago were also racist, yet the validity of newer non-racist genetic etc. explanations is widely accepted today.

Another reason for reflex rejection of geographic explanations is that historians have a tradition, in their discipline, of stressing the role of contingency (a favorite word among historians) based on individual decisions and chance. Often that view is warranted. But often, too, that view is unwarranted. The development of warm fur clothes among the Inuit living north of the Arctic Circle was not because one influential Inuit leader persuaded other Inuit in 1783 to adopt warm fur clothes, for no good environmental reason.

A third reason is that geographic explanations usually depend on detailed technical facts of geography and other fields of scholarship. Most historians and economists don't acquire that detailed knowledge as part of the professional training.

passage_2.text:
RESIDENTS of Lozère, a hilly department in southern France, recite complaints familiar to many rural corners of Europe. In remote hamlets and villages, with names such as Le Bacon and Le Bacon Vieux, mayors grumble about a lack of local schools, jobs, or phone and internet connections. Farmers of grazing animals add another concern: the return of wolves. Eradicated from France last century, the predators are gradually creeping back to more forests and hillsides. "The wolf must be taken in hand," said an aspiring parliamentarian, Francis Palombi, when pressed by voters in an election campaign early this summer. Tourists enjoy visiting a wolf park in Lozère, but farmers fret over their livestock and their livelihoods.

As early as the ninth century, the royal office of the Luparii—wolf-catchers—was created in France to tackle the predators. Those official hunters (and others) completed their job in the 1930s, when the last wolf disappeared from the mainland. Active hunting and improved technology such as rifles in the 19th century, plus the use of poison such as strychnine later on, caused the population collapse. But in the early 1990s the animals reappeared. They crossed the Alps from Italy, upsetting sheep farmers on the French side of the border. Wolves have since spread to areas such as Lozère, delighting environmentalists, who see the predators' presence as a sign of wider ecological health. Farmers, who say the wolves cause the deaths of thousands of sheep and other grazing animals, are less cheerful. They grumble that green activists and politically correct urban types have allowed the return of an old enemy.

Various factors explain the changes of the past few decades. Rural depopulation is part of the story. In Lozère, for example, farming and a once-flourishing mining industry supported a population of over 140,000 residents in the mid-19th century. Today the department has fewer than 80,000 people, many in its towns. As humans withdraw, forests are expanding. In France, between 1990 and 2015, forest cover increased by an average of 102,000 hectares each year, as more fields were given over to trees. Now, nearly one-third of mainland France is covered by woodland of some sort. The decline of hunting as a sport also means more forests fall quiet. In the mid-to-late 20th century over 2m hunters regularly spent winter weekends tramping in woodland, seeking boars, birds and other prey. Today the Fédération Nationale des Chasseurs, the national body, claims 1.1m people hold hunting licences, though the number of active hunters is probably lower. The mostly protected status of the wolf in Europe—hunting them is now forbidden, other than when occasional culls are sanctioned by the state—plus the efforts of NGOs to track and count the animals, also contribute to the recovery of wolf populations.

As the lupine population of Europe spreads westwards, with occasional reports of wolves seen closer to urban areas, expect to hear of more clashes between farmers and those who celebrate the predators' return. Farmers' losses are real, but are not the only economic story. Tourist venues, such as parks where wolves are kept and the animals' spread is discussed, also generate income and jobs in rural areas.

passage_3.text:
For early postcolonial literature, the world of the novel was often the nation. Postcolonial novels were usually concerned with national questions. Sometimes the whole story of the novel was taken as an allegory of the nation, whether India or Tanzania. This was important for supporting anti-colonial nationalism, but could also be limiting - land-focused and inward- looking.

My new book "Writing Ocean Worlds" explores another kind of world of the novel: not the village or nation, but the Indian Ocean world. The book describes a set of novels in which the Indian Ocean is at the centre of the story. It focuses on the novelists Amitav Ghosh, Abdulrazak Gurnah, Lindsey Collen and Joseph Conrad who have centred the Indian Ocean world in the majority of their novels. Their work reveals a world that is outward-looking -full of movement, border-crossing and south-south interconnection. They are all very different – from colonially inclined (Conrad) to radically anti-capitalist (Collen), but together draw on and shape a wider sense of Indian Ocean space through themes, images, metaphors and language. This has the effect of remapping the world in the reader's mind, as centred in the interconnected global south.

The Indian Ocean world is a term used to describe the very long-lasting connections among the coasts of East Africa, the Arab coasts, and South and East Asia. These connections were made possible by the geography of the Indian Ocean. For much of history, travel by sea was much easier than by land, which meant that port cities very far apart were often more easily connected to each other than to much closer inland cities. Historical and archaeological evidence suggests that what we now call globalisation first appeared in the Indian Ocean.

This is the interconnected oceanic world referenced and produced by the novels in my book. For their part Ghosh, Gurnah, Collen and even Conrad reference a different set of histories and geographies than the ones most commonly found in fiction in English. Those commonly found ones are mostly centred in Europe or the US, assume a background of Christianity and whiteness, and mention places like Paris and New York. The novels in my book highlight instead a largely Islamic space, feature characters of colour and centralise the ports of Malindi, Mombasa, Aden, Java and Bombay.

It is a densely imagined, richly sensory image of a southern cosmopolitan culture which provides for an enlarged sense of place in the world. This remapping is particularly powerful for the representation of Africa. In the fiction, sailors and travellers are not all European. African, as well as Indian and Arab characters, are traders, nakhodas (dhow ship captains), runaways, villains, missionaries and activists. This does not mean that Indian Ocean Africa is romanticised. Migration is often a matter of force; travel is portrayed as abandonment rather than adventure, freedoms are kept from women and slavery is rife. What it does mean is that the African part of the Indian Ocean world plays an active role in its long, rich history and therefore in that of the wider world.

passage_4.text:
Fifty years after its publication in English in 1972, and just a year since Marshall Sahlins himself died—we may ask: why did his essay "Original Affluent Society" have such an impact, and how has it fared since? Sahlins's principal argument was simple but counterintuitive: before being driven into marginal environments by colonial powers, hunter-gatherers, or foragers, were not engaged in a desperate struggle for meager survival. Quite the contrary, they satisfied their needs with far less work than people in agricultural and industrial societies, leaving them more time to use as they wished. Hunters, he quipped, keep bankers' hours. Refusing to maximize, many were "more concerned with games of chance than with chances of game." The so-called Neolithic Revolution, rather than improving life, imposed a harsher work regime and set in motion the long history of growing inequality.

Moreover, foragers had other options. The contemporary Hadza of Tanzania, who had long been surrounded by farmers, knew they had alternatives and rejected them. To Sahlins, this showed that foragers are not simply examples of human diversity or victimhood but something more profound: they demonstrated that societies make real choices. Culture, a way of living oriented around a distinctive set of values, manifests a fundamental principle of collective self-determination.

But the point of the essay is not so much the empirical validity of the data the real interest for most readers, after all, is not in foragers either today or in the Paleolithic but rather its conceptual challenge to contemporary economic life and bourgeois individualism. The empirical served a philosophical and political project, a thought experiment and stimulus to the imagination of possibilities.

With its title's nod toward The Affluent Society (1958), economist John Kenneth Galbraith's famously skeptical portrait of America's postwar prosperity and inequality, and dripping with New Left contempt for consumerism, "The Original Affluent Society" brought this critical perspective to bear on the contemporary world. It did so through the classic anthropological move of showing that radical alternatives to the readers' lives really exist. If the capitalist world seeks wealth through ever greater material production to meet infinitely expansive desires, foraging societies follow "the Zen road to affluence": not by getting more, but by wanting less. If it seems that foragers have been left behind by "progress," this is due only to the ethnocentric self-congratulation of the West. Rather than accumulate material goods, these societies are guided by other values: leisure, mobility, and above all, freedom.

Viewed in today's context, of course, not every aspect of the essay has aged well. While acknowledging the violence of colonialism, racism, and dispossession, it does not thematize them as heavily as might be expected today. Rebuking evolutionary anthropologists for treating present-day foragers as "left behind" by progress, it too can succumb to the temptation to use them as proxies for the Paleolithic. Yet these characteristics should not distract us from appreciating Sahlins's effort to show that if we want to conjure new possibilities, we need to learn about actually inhabitable worlds.

questions.question_text: All of the following can be inferred from the passage EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: several academic studies of human phenomena in the past involved racist interpretations.

options.label: B
options.text: agricultural practices changed drastically in the Australian continent after it was colonised.

options.label: C
options.text: while most human phenomena result from culture and individual choice, some have bio-geographic origins.

options.label: D
options.text: individual dictat and contingency were not the causal factors for the use of fur clothing in some very cold climates.

questions.explanation_text:
Process: Since this asks for what we cannot infer, we need to find the option that goes beyond what the passage actually says or makes claims the passage doesn't support.

From passage: "Many human phenomena and characteristics are influenced both by geographic factors and by non-geographic factors."

The author gives examples of both types -> doesn't rank them or say which affects most phenomena. The passage shows geographic factors matter (Inuit fur clothes, Australian agriculture) and non-geographic factors matter (North vs South Korea) but never quantifies which dominates.

Elimination Process:

🔴 Option 1 -> directly supported -> passage clearly states "some geographic explanations advanced a century ago were racist" and "many genetic, historical, psychological, and anthropological explanations advanced a century ago were also racist"

🔴 Option 2 -> directly supported -> passage explains Australia went from "no indigenous farming" (hunter/gatherers only) to using "non-native species such as sheep, wheat, and grapes, brought to Australia by overseas colonists"

🟢 Option 3 -> degree-error -> uses words "most" and "some" to rank factors, but passage never makes this quantitative claim. It only says "many phenomena are influenced by both" types of factors

🔴 Option 4 -> directly supported -> passage explicitly states Inuit fur development was "not because one influential Inuit leader persuaded others" but due to "straightforward geographic" reasons

Key confusion students face: Options 1, 2, and 4 feel clearly supported, but Option 3 sounds reasonable because the passage does discuss both geographic and cultural factors.

The trap: Option 3 makes a ranking claim (most vs some) that the passage never makes. The passage shows both factors matter but doesn't say which dominates.

Answer: Option 3

questions.question_text: The author criticises scholars who are not geographers for all of the following reasons EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: the importance they place on the role of individual decisions when studying human phenomena.

options.label: B
options.text: their outdated interpretations of past cultural and historical phenomena.

options.label: C
options.text: their labelling of geographic explanations as deterministic.

options.label: D
options.text: their rejection of the role of biogeographic factors in social and cultural phenomena.

questions.explanation_text:
Need to find criticisms the author actually makes, then spot the exception.

From passage: "But many scholars do react to any explanation invoking some geographic role, by denouncing 'geographic determinism'"

From passage: "historians have a tradition, in their discipline, of stressing the role of contingency based on individual decisions and chance. Often that view is warranted. But often, too, that view is unwarranted"

Author's main criticisms -> scholars reject geographic explanations -> call them "deterministic" -> overemphasize individual choices -> ignore biogeographic factors like Australia's lack of domesticable species.

But wait -> when author mentions "outdated interpretations," they're actually explaining why scholars unfairly reject geographic explanations -> not criticizing scholars for being outdated themselves.

🟠 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> author does criticize overemphasis on individual decisions, calling this view "often unwarranted" when applied to things like Inuit fur clothes

🟢 Option 2 -> correct answer -> author mentions racist explanations from a century ago but uses this to explain unfair rejection of geography, not to criticize scholars for being outdated

🟠 Option 3 -> partial-truth -> author directly criticizes scholars for "denouncing geographic determinism" as a reflex reaction

🟠 Option 4 -> partial-truth -> author criticizes rejection of biogeographic factors, using Aboriginal Australia example where scholars ignore obvious geographic reasons for lack of agriculture

The confusion here -> students might think option 2 is a criticism because author mentions old racist theories. But read carefully -> author uses this to defend geography by showing other fields also had racist pasts but moved forward. Author isn't criticizing scholars for being outdated -> just explaining their unfair bias against geography.

questions.question_text: All of the following are advanced by the author as reasons why non-geographers disregard geographic influences on human phenomena EXCEPT their:

options.label: A
options.text: belief in the central role of humans, unrelated to physical surroundings, in influencing phenomena.

options.label: B
options.text: disciplinary training which typically does not include technical knowledge of geography.

options.label: C
options.text: dismissal of explanations that involve geographical causes for human behaviour.

options.label: D
options.text: lingering impressions of past geographic analyses that were politically offensive.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what the passage does NOT mention as a reason why scholars reject geographic explanations.

From passage: "Several reasons may underlie this widespread but nonsensical view..."

The author lists three specific reasons why non-geographers reject geographic explanations:

Reason 1: Racist history -> Past geographic explanations were racist, so all geographic explanations now seem tainted

Reason 2: Historical tradition -> Historians stress "contingency" based on individual decisions and chance (belief in central role of humans)

Reason 3: Lack of training -> Geographic explanations need technical knowledge that historians/economists don't get in their training

Key insight: The passage says scholars react by "denouncing geographic determinism" - but this doesn't mean they dismiss geographic explanations entirely. They just label any geographic explanation as "determinism."

🟠 Option 1 -> mentioned -> The passage talks about historians stressing "individual decisions and chance" which shows belief in central human role

🟠 Option 2 -> mentioned -> Passage directly states "Most historians and economists don't acquire that detailed knowledge as part of professional training"

🟢 Option 3 -> NOT mentioned -> The passage never says scholars dismiss geographic explanations. It says they denounce "geographic determinism" when geographic factors are mentioned, which is different from dismissal

🟠 Option 4 -> mentioned -> Passage explicitly states geographic explanations became "tainted by racist associations"

The passage describes scholars' reaction to geographic explanations (denouncing them as determinism), not their dismissal of such explanations completely.

questions.question_text: The examples of the Inuit and Aboriginal Australians are offered in the passage to show

options.label: A
options.text: how physical circumstances can dictate human behaviour and cultures.

options.label: B
options.text: how environmental factors lead to comparatively divergent paths in livelihoods and development

options.label: C
options.text: that despite geographical isolation, traditional societies were self-sufficient and adaptive.

options.label: D
options.text: human resourcefulness across cultures in adapting to their surroundings

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "The explanation is straightforwardly geographic, rather than a cultural or historical quirk unrelated to geography" and "The explanation is biogeographic: the Australian continent has no domesticable native animal species"

The passage uses these examples to show geographic factors directly controlling human development -> Inuit developed fur clothes because of Arctic climate (had to) -> Aboriginal Australians stayed hunter-gatherers because continent lacked domesticable species (couldn't farm) -> both show environment forcing certain outcomes.

Students often get confused between options 1 and 2 because both mention environmental influence. Here's how to eliminate:

🟢 Option 1 -> correct -> captures the dictating power of physical circumstances -> matches passage's emphasis on geographic determinism (environment forces specific behaviors)

🟠 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> mentions environmental influence correctly but focuses on divergent paths rather than the controlling power of geography -> misses the deterministic aspect

🔴 Option 3 -> scope-error -> talks about being "self-sufficient and adaptive despite isolation" -> passage shows they developed because of geography, not despite it

🔴 Option 4 -> context-shift -> emphasizes human resourcefulness -> passage emphasizes geographic control, not human creativity in adapting

Key distinction: Option 1 shows geography as the boss telling humans what to do -> Option 2 just shows different results from different places (weaker connection to the passage's main point about geographic determinism).

questions.question_text: Which one of the following has NOT contributed to the growing wolf population in Lozère?

options.label: A
options.text: The shutting down of the royal office of the Luparii.

options.label: B
options.text: The granting of a protected status to wolves in Europe.

options.label: C
options.text: An increase in woodlands and forest cover in Lozère.

options.label: D
options.text: A decline in the rural population of Lozère.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "Various factors explain the changes of the past few decades. Rural depopulation is part of the story... As humans withdraw, forests are expanding... The mostly protected status of the wolf in Europe... plus the efforts of NGOs to track and count the animals, also contribute to the recovery of wolf populations."

The passage clearly lists modern factors -> rural depopulation -> forest expansion -> protected status -> NGO efforts. But the Luparii office is only mentioned as history, not as a current contributing factor.

🟢 Option 1 is correct -> The Luparii office is mentioned only as historical context (9th century creation, job completed in 1930s). Passage doesn't connect its shutdown to current wolf recovery.

🔴 Option 2 -> directly contradicts passage -> "The mostly protected status of the wolf in Europe... contribute to the recovery of wolf populations" - clearly stated as a factor

🔴 Option 3 -> directly contradicts passage -> "forests are expanding... forest cover increased by an average of 102,000 hectares each year" - clearly linked to wolf return

🔴 Option 4 -> directly contradicts passage -> "Rural depopulation is part of the story" - explicitly mentioned as contributing factor

Key insight: Don't confuse historical background with current contributing factors. The passage mentions Luparii as why wolves disappeared historically, but never says shutting it down helped them return.

questions.question_text: The inhabitants of Lozère have to grapple with all of the following problems, EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: lack of educational facilities.

options.label: B
options.text: livestock losses.

options.label: C
options.text: poor rural communication infrastructure.

options.label: D
options.text: decline in the number of hunting licences.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "mayors grumble about a lack of local schools, jobs, or phone and internet connections. Farmers of grazing animals add another concern: the return of wolves."

The key is to identify what the passage actually says Lozère residents complain about -> then find what's not on their list of problems.

The passage clearly lists their complaints: no schools, no jobs, bad internet/phone, and wolf attacks on livestock.we need to check if hunting license decline is mentioned as their problem.

🟢 Option 1 -> directly stated -> "lack of local schools" is explicitly mentioned as something mayors grumble about

🟢 Option 2 -> directly stated -> wolves cause "deaths of thousands of sheep and other grazing animals" - farmers are upset about this

🟢 Option 3 -> directly stated -> "lack of phone and internet connections" is specifically mentioned as a complaint

🔴 Option 4 -> context-shift -> hunting license decline is mentioned as a general France trend that helps wolves recover, but it's never presented as something Lozère residents are struggling with as a problem

The passage mentions hunting decline as background information explaining why wolves returned, not as something residents complain about. The residents' actual complaints are very specific and listed clearly in the first paragraph.

questions.question_text: The author presents a possible economic solution to an existing issue facing Lozère that takes into account the divergent and competing interests of:

options.label: A
options.text: environmentalists and politicians.

options.label: B
options.text: tourists and environmentalists.

options.label: C
options.text: politicians and farmers.

options.label: D
options.text: farmers and environmentalists.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find where the author suggests an economic solution that balances competing interests between two groups.

Step-by-step process:

First, identify the main conflict -> Farmers hate wolves (kill livestock) vs. Environmentalists love wolves (ecological health sign)

Next, find the economic solution -> Look for where author suggests how to make money despite this conflict

Finally, check which groups have competing interests that this solution addresses

From passage: "Farmers' losses are real, but are not the only economic story. Tourist venues, such as parks where wolves are kept and the animals' spread is discussed, also generate income and jobs in rural areas."

Thought process:

Author acknowledges farmers lose money from wolves -> but then suggests wolf tourism can create jobs and income -> this tries to balance both sides of the conflict -> farmers want wolves gone (economic loss) vs environmentalists want wolves to stay (ecological benefit) -> tourism solution gives economic benefit while keeping wolves

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> Politicians aren't shown having competing economic interests about wolves in the passage

🔴 Option 2 -> context-shift -> Tourists and environmentalists aren't in conflict - they both benefit from wolves being around

🔴 Option 3 -> scope-error -> Politicians aren't presented as having divergent interests from farmers specifically about this wolf issue

🟢 Option 4 is correct -> captures the exact conflict described: farmers lose money from wolves killing livestock while environmentalists want wolves for ecological reasons, and tourism solution tries to address both concerns

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements, if true, would weaken the author's claims?

options.label: A
options.text: The old mining sites of Lozère are now being used as grazing pastures for sheep.

options.label: B
options.text: Having migrated out in the last century, wolves are now returning to Lozère.

options.label: C
options.text: Unemployment concerns the residents of Lozère.

options.label: D
options.text: Wolf attacks on tourists in Lozère are on the rise.

questions.explanation_text:
Find what would weaken the author's main claims about wolves returning to France.

Step 1: Identify the author's key claims

The author presents a balanced view of wolf return:

  • Farmers worry about livestock deaths
  • Environmentalists see wolves as good for nature
  • Tourism from wolves brings money to rural areas

From passage: "Tourist venues, such as parks where wolves are kept and the animals' spread is discussed, also generate income and jobs in rural areas."

Step 2: Find what weakens these claims

To weaken -> look for something that makes the author's arguments less convincing

Author says wolves bring tourism benefits -> What would hurt this claim? -> Tourist safety problems!

Option Analysis:

🟠 Option 1 -> irrelevant -> Mining sites becoming pastures has nothing to do with the wolf debate. Doesn't touch any main claims.

🟠 Option 2 -> supports-author -> This actually agrees with what the passage says! Doesn't weaken anything.

🟠 Option 3 -> off-topic -> Unemployment is briefly mentioned but isn't central to wolf arguments. Doesn't weaken the core claims.

🟢 Option 4 -> weakens-key-claim -> If wolves attack tourists, this destroys the author's point about tourism benefits. Makes wolves seem more dangerous than the author suggests.

Elimination trick: Options 1-3 either agree with the passage or talk about unrelated topics. Only Option 4 directly contradicts a positive claim the author makes about wolves (tourism benefits).

questions.question_text: All of the following statements, if true, would weaken the passage's claim about the relationship between mainstream English-language fiction and Indian Ocean novels EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: the depiction of Africa in most Indian Ocean novels is driven by a postcolonial nostalgia for an idyllic past.

options.label: B
options.text: the depiction of Africa in most Indian Ocean novels is driven by an Orientalist imagination of its cultural crudeness.

options.label: C
options.text: most mainstream English-language novels have historically privileged the Christian, white, male experience of travel and adventure.

options.label: D
options.text: very few mainstream English-language novels have historically been set in American and European metropolitan centres.

questions.explanation_text:
Understanding the passage's main claim: The author contrasts mainstream English fiction with Indian Ocean novels. Mainstream fiction is described as Europe/US-centered, assuming "Christianity and whiteness," mentioning places like "Paris and New York." Indian Ocean novels offer a different perspective - featuring "largely Islamic space" and "characters of colour."

From passage: "Those commonly found ones are mostly centred in Europe or the US, assume a background of Christianity and whiteness, and mention places like Paris and New York. The novels in my book highlight instead a largely Islamic space, feature characters of colour..."

The key insight -> We need the statement that supports rather than weakens this contrast.

🟠 Option 1 -> weakens the claim -> Says Indian Ocean novels show "postcolonial nostalgia for an idyllic past" which contradicts the passage's point that "Indian Ocean Africa is not romanticised"

🟠 Option 2 -> weakens the claim -> Says Indian Ocean novels use "Orientalist imagination" which would make them similar to problematic mainstream fiction, not different

🟢 Option 3 -> supports the claim -> Says mainstream fiction "privileged the Christian, white, male experience" which perfectly matches the passage's description of mainstream fiction as assuming "Christianity and whiteness"

🟠 Option 4 -> weakens the claim -> Says "very few" mainstream novels are set in American/European centers, but the passage claims they mention "places like Paris and New York"

Option 3 actually reinforces the passage's characterization of mainstream English fiction instead of challenging it. It's the exception that supports rather than weakens.

questions.question_text: All of the following claims contribute to the "remapping" discussed by the passage, EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: Indian Ocean novels have gone beyond the specifics of national concerns to explore rich regional pasts.

options.label: B
options.text: the global south, as opposed to the global north, was the first centre of globalisation.

options.label: C
options.text: the world of early international trade and commerce was not the sole domain of white Europeans.

options.label: D
options.text: cosmopolitanism originated in the West and travelled to the East through globalization

questions.explanation_text:
To solve this question,we need to understand what "remapping" means in the passage, then find which option goes against this idea.

From passage: "This has the effect of remapping the world in the reader's mind, as centred in the interconnected global south."

The passage explains that these novels shift focus away from Euro-centric stories -> toward Indian Ocean world stories. They challenge the usual focus on Europe/US -> by highlighting Africa, Arabia, and Asia instead.

From passage: "reference a different set of histories and geographies than the ones most commonly found in fiction in English. Those commonly found ones are mostly centred in Europe or the US"

So remapping = changing from Western-centered view -> to global south-centered view

Now let's check which option does NOT support this remapping:

🟢 Option 1 -> supports remapping -> moves beyond narrow national focus to explore broader regional connections (exactly what passage describes)

🟢 Option 2 -> supports remapping -> puts global south first in globalization history, challenging Euro-centric narrative

🟢 Option 3 -> supports remapping -> shows non-Europeans as active traders, not just Europeans (passage mentions African, Arab traders)

🔴 Option 4 -> contradicts remapping -> says cosmopolitanism started in West and went East. This is exactly the opposite of what the passage argues! The passage shows the Indian Ocean world (East/South) had rich cosmopolitan culture first

Option 4 reinforces Western-centric thinking instead of challenging it, so it does NOT contribute to remapping.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements is not true about migration in the Indian Ocean world?

options.label: A
options.text: Geographical location rather than geographical proximity determined the choice of destination for migrants.

options.label: B
options.text: The Indian Ocean world's migration networks were shaped by religious and commercial histories of the region.

options.label: C
options.text: Migration in the Indian Ocean world was an ambivalent experience.

options.label: D
options.text: The Indian Ocean world's migration networks connected the global north with the global south.

questions.explanation_text:
Need to find what the passage actually says about migration patterns and connections.

From passage: "Their work reveals a world that is outward-looking - full of movement, border-crossing and south-south interconnection... This has the effect of remapping the world in the reader's mind, as centred in the interconnected global south."

The key insight -> passage emphasizes south-south connections, not north-south connections. The Indian Ocean world is presented as separate from European/US-centered narratives.

From passage: "For much of history, travel by sea was much easier than by land, which meant that port cities very far apart were often more easily connected to each other than to much closer inland cities."

This shows geography (being a port) mattered more than proximity -> supports option 1 as true.

🟢 Option 1 -> TRUE -> passage clearly states port cities far apart connected better than nearby inland cities due to sea travel ease

🟢 Option 2 -> TRUE -> passage mentions "largely Islamic space" (religious) and traders/nakhodas (commercial) shaping the region

🟢 Option 3 -> TRUE -> passage says migration was "often a matter of force" and "portrayed as abandonment rather than adventure" but also mentions rich history -> shows mixed/ambivalent experience

🔴 Option 4 -> FALSE -> passage emphasizes "south-south interconnection" and contrasts Indian Ocean world against Europe/US-centered narratives, not connecting with them

The confusion might be thinking the Indian Ocean world connected everything globally. But the passage specifically contrasts it against the global north (Europe/US), focusing on connections within the global south instead.

questions.question_text: On the basis of the nature of the relationship between the items in each pair below, choose the odd pair out:

options.label: A
options.text: Indian Ocean world : Slavery

options.label: B
options.text: Indian Ocean novels : Outward-looking

options.label: C
options.text: Postcolonial novels : Border-crossing

options.label: D
options.text: Postcolonial novels: Anti-colonial nationalism

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find which pair has a different type of relationship compared to the others.

Step 1: Check what the passage says about each relationship

For Indian Ocean world and slavery -> passage mentions slavery exists there

For Indian Ocean novels and outward-looking -> passage directly calls them outward-looking

For postcolonial novels and border-crossing -> need to check this carefully

For postcolonial novels and anti-colonial nationalism -> passage connects these

Step 2: Look for the mismatch

The key is finding where the passage says the opposite or assigns a quality to a different category.

From passage: "This was important for supporting anti-colonial nationalism, but could also be limiting - land-focused and inward-looking" (about postcolonial novels)

From passage: "Their work reveals a world that is outward-looking -full of movement, border-crossing and south-south interconnection" (about Indian Ocean novels)

Thought process: Postcolonial novels = inward-looking -> Border-crossing = Indian Ocean novels -> So postcolonial novels and border-crossing don't match!

🟢 Option 1 -> correct pairing -> Indian Ocean world does have slavery according to passage

🟢 Option 2 -> correct pairing -> Indian Ocean novels are directly called "outward-looking"

🔴 Option 3 -> mismatched pairing -> border-crossing belongs to Indian Ocean novels, but postcolonial novels are called "inward-looking" and "land-focused"

🟢 Option 4 -> correct pairing -> passage clearly links postcolonial novels to anti-colonial nationalism

The odd pair is Option 3 because it wrongly connects border-crossing (which belongs to Indian Ocean novels) with postcolonial novels (which are described as inward-looking).

questions.question_text: The author of the passage mentions Galbraith's "The Affluent Society" to:

options.label: A
options.text: show how Galbraith's theories refute Sahlins's thesis on the contentment of pre-hunter- gatherer communities.

options.label: B
options.text: document the influence of Galbraith's cynical views on modern consumerism on Sahlins's analysis of pre-historic societies.

options.label: C
options.text: contrast the materialist nature of contemporary growth paths with the pacifist content ways of living among the foragers.

options.label: D
options.text: show how Sahlins's views complemented Galbraith's criticism of the consumerism and inequality of contemporary society.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find why the author brings up Galbraith's book when discussing Sahlins's essay.

From passage: "With its title's nod toward The Affluent Society (1958), economist John Kenneth Galbraith's famously skeptical portrait of America's postwar prosperity and inequality, and dripping with New Left contempt for consumerism, 'The Original Affluent Society' brought this critical perspective to bear on the contemporary world."

The key insight -> Both writers share the same critical view of modern consumerism and inequality. Sahlins even named his essay as a "nod" to Galbraith's work.

The passage shows -> Galbraith criticized postwar prosperity and inequality -> Sahlins also criticized contemporary economic life -> Both attack consumerism -> They work together, not against each other.

Many students get stuck between these because both mention Galbraith's views on consumerism. Here's how to tell them apart:

🟠 Option 1 -> opposite-direction -> Says Galbraith "refutes" Sahlins, but passage shows they agree and share critical views

🟠 Option 2 -> scope-error -> Focuses on "influence on analysis of pre-historic societies" but passage talks about their shared criticism of contemporary society, not prehistoric analysis

🟠 Option 3 -> wrong-focus -> Mentions "pacifist content" but passage emphasizes "leisure, mobility, and freedom" - not pacifism specifically

🟢 Option 4 -> correct -> Captures that both writers complement each other in criticizing modern consumerism and inequality

The elimination trick: Look for the word "complement" vs "refute" vs "influence." The passage uses language showing agreement between the two thinkers, not disagreement or one-way influence.

questions.question_text: The author mentions Tanzania's Hadza community to illustrate:

options.label: A
options.text: that hunter-gatherer communities' subsistence-level techniques equipped them to survive well into contemporary times.

options.label: B
options.text: how pre-agrarian societies did not hamper the emergence of more advanced agrarian practices in contiguous communities.

options.label: C
options.text: how two vastly different ways of living and working were able to coexist in proximity for centuries.

options.label: D
options.text: that forager communities' lifestyles derived not from ignorance about alternatives, but from their own choice.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "The contemporary Hadza of Tanzania, who had long been surrounded by farmers, knew they had alternatives and rejected them. To Sahlins, this showed that foragers are not simply examples of human diversity or victimhood but something more profound: they demonstrated that societies make real choices."

The key insight here is: Hadza knew about farming (they were surrounded by farmers) -> but they chose to reject it -> this proves foragers make real choices about their lifestyle.

The author uses Hadza to counter the idea that foragers live the way they do because they don't know better. Instead, it shows they make informed decisions about how to live.

🟠 Option 1 -> scope-error -> talks about "survival techniques" but passage uses Hadza to show choice, not survival ability. Misses the main point about decision-making.

🔴 Option 2 -> irrelevant -> discusses how foragers don't "hamper" agricultural development. Passage doesn't mention this relationship at all - focuses on choice, not impact on others.

🟠 Option 3 -> partial-truth -> correctly notes they lived near each other, but misses the core point. Passage isn't about coexistence - it's about Hadza choosing their lifestyle despite knowing alternatives.

🟢 Option 4 -> captures the complete argument -> directly matches the passage logic: they knew alternatives existed but chose their own way, proving lifestyle comes from choice, not ignorance.

questions.question_text: The author of the passage criticises Sahlins's essay for its:

options.label: A
options.text: failure to supplement its thesis with robust empirical data.

options.label: B
options.text: outdated values regarding present-day foragers versus ancient foraging communities.

options.label: C
options.text: cursory treatment of the effects of racism and colonialism on societies.

options.label: D
options.text: critique of anthropologists who disparage the choices of foragers in today's society.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find where the author actually criticizes Sahlins's essay, not where the author describes what Sahlins argued.

The key is to find the critical section where the author points out flaws in the essay.

From passage: "Viewed in today's context, of course, not every aspect of the essay has aged well. While acknowledging the violence of colonialism, racism, and dispossession, it does not thematize them as heavily as might be expected today."

The criticism is clear -> The essay doesn't give enough attention to colonialism, racism, and dispossession by today's standards -> This means the treatment was too light or cursory.

Elimination process:

🔴 Option 1 -> irrelevant -> The passage actually says the essay's point was not empirical validity but philosophical challenge. No criticism about lacking data.

🔴 Option 2 -> context-shift -> The passage mentions using present-day foragers as "proxies for Paleolithic" but doesn't call this "outdated values." Wrong framing.

🟢 Option 3 -> correct -> "cursory treatment" perfectly matches "does not thematize them as heavily as might be expected today"

🔴 Option 4 -> backwards -> This describes what Sahlins did (critiqued other anthropologists), not what he's criticized for

The confusion might come from Option 2 since the passage mentions both present-day and Paleolithic foragers. But the criticism isn't about "outdated values" -> it's about using present-day groups as stand-ins for ancient ones, which is different.

Option 3 directly matches the author's words about not giving enough attention to colonialism and racism.

questions.question_text: We can infer that Sahlins's main goal in writing his essay was to:

options.label: A
options.text: put forth the view that, despite egalitarian origins, economic progress brings greater inequality and social hierarchies.

options.label: B
options.text: hold a mirror to an acquisitive society, with examples of other communities that have chosen successfully to be non-materialistic.

options.label: C
options.text: counter Galbraith's pessimistic view of the inevitability of a capitalist trajectory for economic growth.

options.label: D
options.text: highlight the fact that while we started off as a fairly contented egalitarian people, we have progressively degenerated into materialism.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find Sahlins's main goal in writing his essay. Let us trace through the passage to understand his purpose.

From passage: "the real interest for most readers, after all, is not in foragers either today or in the Paleolithic—but rather its conceptual challenge to contemporary economic life and bourgeois individualism. The empirical served a philosophical and political project"

This tells us -> Sahlins wasn't just describing foragers for academic interest -> he wanted to challenge how we think about modern economic life.

From passage: "It did so through the classic anthropological move of showing that radical alternatives to the readers' lives really exist. If the capitalist world seeks wealth through ever greater material production to meet infinitely expansive desires, foraging societies follow 'the Zen road to affluence': not by getting more, but by wanting less."

This shows us -> Sahlins used foraging societies as examples -> to show there are other ways to live -> specifically non-materialistic ways -> this creates a "mirror" effect for our acquisitive society.

🔴 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> mentions inequality correctly but misses the main point. Sahlins wasn't just making a historical argument about progress causing inequality -> he was using this to challenge current society.

🟢 Option 2 -> correct -> captures both the "mirror" function (challenging acquisitive society) and the method (showing non-materialistic alternatives that work).

🔴 Option 3 -> context-shift -> completely wrong about Galbraith. The passage says Sahlins's title nodded to Galbraith and brought a similar critical perspective -> they were aligned, not opposing each other.

🟠 Option 4 -> scope-error -> focuses only on the historical narrative (how we "degenerated") but misses the main goal -> which was to challenge contemporary society by showing working alternatives.

The key insight: Sahlins used foraging societies not just to tell history, but as working examples to challenge how we live today.

questions.question_text:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide where (option 1, 2, 3, or 4) the following sentence would best fit.

Paragraph: The experience of reading philosophy is often disquieting. When reading philosophy, the values around which one has heretofore organised one's life may come to look provincial, flatly wrong, or even evil ___ (1) ___ . When beliefs previously held as truths are rendered implausible, new beliefs, values, and ways of living may be required ___ (2) ___ . What's worse, philosophers admonish each other to remain unsutured until such time as a defensible new answer is revealed or constructed. Sometimes philosophical writing is even strictly critical in that it does not even attempt to provide an alternative after tearing down a cultural or conceptual citadel ___ (3) ___ . The reader of philosophy must be prepared for the possibility of this experience. While reading philosophy can help one clarify one's values, and even make one self-conscious for the first time of the fact that there are good reasons for believing what one believes, it can also generate unremediated doubt that is difficult to live with ___ (4) ___ .

Sentence: This philosophical cut at one's core beliefs, values, and way of life is difficult enough.

options.label: A
options.text: Option 1

options.label: B
options.text: Option 2

options.label: C
options.text: Option 3

options.label: D
options.text: Option 4

questions.explanation_text:
The missing sentence talks about a "philosophical cut" being "difficult enough" -> this suggests it's summarizing or emphasizing difficulty already mentioned.

From passage: "When beliefs previously held as truths are rendered implausible, new beliefs, values, and ways of living may be required"

Key clue: The word "This" in our sentence points backward -> it refers to something already described. Need to find what "this philosophical cut" refers to.

Process: Look at each spot -> does the sentence make sense flowing from what's before it?

🟠 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> comes after values looking "wrong or evil" but the word "This" doesn't have a clear reference to a "cut" yet

🟢 Option 2 -> perfect fit -> follows the description of beliefs being "rendered implausible" and needing new ones. The word "This" clearly refers to this challenging process of philosophical questioning

🟠 Option 3 -> context-shift -> comes after talking about critical writing that tears down without alternatives. While related, "This" doesn't flow as naturally from the tearing down idea

🔴 Option 4 -> scope-error -> comes after describing both positive and negative effects. The sentence emphasizes difficulty, but here we're already moving to a balanced conclusion about philosophy's mixed effects

The sentence fits best after describing how beliefs become implausible and new ones are needed -> that's exactly the "philosophical cut" being referenced.

questions.question_text:
There is a sentence that is missing in the paragraph below. Look at the paragraph and decide where (option 1, 2, 3, or 4) the following sentence would best fit.

Paragraph: The researchers also uncovered an unexpected genetic link between Native Americans and Japanese people ___ (1) ___ . During the deglaciation period, another group branched out from northern coastal China and travelled to Japan ___ (2) ___ . "We were surprised to find that this ancestral source also contributed to the Japanese gene pool, especially the indigenous Ainus," says Li ___ (3) ___ . They shared similarities in how they crafted stemmed projectile points for arrowheads and spears ___ (4) ___ . "This suggests that the Pleistocene connection among the Americas, China, and Japan was not confined to culture but also to genetics," says senior author Qing-Peng Kong, an evolutionary geneticist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

Sentence: The discovery helps to explain archeological similarities between the Paleolithic peoples of China, Japan, and the Americas.

options.label: A
options.text: Option 1

options.label: B
options.text: Option 2

options.label: C
options.text: Option 3

options.label: D
options.text: Option 4

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "The researchers also uncovered an unexpected genetic link between Native Americans and Japanese people... 'We were surprised to find that this ancestral source also contributed to the Japanese gene pool, especially the indigenous Ainus,' says Li... They shared similarities in how they crafted stemmed projectile points for arrowheads and spears"

The key insight: The sentence talks about how "the discovery helps to explain archeological similarities" -> This means it should come after the genetic discoveries are explained but before the specific archaeological evidence is mentioned.

Flow analysis: Genetic findings -> Transition sentence about archaeology -> Specific archaeological example -> Final conclusion

🔴 Option 1 -> too-early -> The genetic discoveries aren't fully explained yet, so mentioning how "the discovery" explains archaeology is premature

🔴 Option 2 -> context-shift -> Still talking about migration patterns, not ready to connect to archaeology yet

🟢 Option 3 -> perfect-transition -> All genetic findings are complete, now we can bridge to archaeology before giving the specific example

🟠 Option 4 -> too-late -> The archaeological evidence (projectile points) is already mentioned, so explaining how discoveries relate to archaeology comes after the fact

Think of it like this: First tell me all your discoveries -> Then tell me what these discoveries explain -> Then give me the specific example -> Then conclude

Position 3 is the perfect bridge between the genetic findings and the archaeological evidence that follows.

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. In English, there is no systematic rule for the naming of numbers; after ten, we have "eleven" and "twelve" and then the teens: "thirteen", "fourteen", "fifteen" and so on.
  2. Even more confusingly, some English words invert the numbers they refer to: the word "fourteen" puts the four first, even though it appears last.
  3. It can take children a while to learn all these words, and understand that "fourteen" is different from "forty".
  4. For multiples of 10, English speakers switch to a different pattern: "twenty", "thirty", "forty" and so on.
  5. If you didn't know the word for "eleven", you would be unable to just guess it - you might come up with something like "one-teen".
questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "In English, there is no systematic rule for the naming of numbers" and "If you didn't know the word for 'eleven', you would be unable to just guess it"

The main theme here is about how English number words are weird and don't follow patterns -> this makes the language confusing structurally.

Step-by-step elimination process:

Sentences 1, 2, 4, 5 all talk about -> structural problems with English number naming:

  • Sentence 1: No systematic rules exist
  • Sentence 2: Words are inverted confusingly
  • Sentence 4: Different patterns are used
  • Sentence 5: You can't guess unknown number words

But sentence 3 talks about -> children learning these words and getting confused between "fourteen" and "forty"

The key difference: Most sentences discuss why English number system is structurally confusing, but sentence 3 shifts to how this affects learners.

🟢 Sentence 3 is the odd one out -> scope-shift -> moves from discussing structural irregularities of English numbers to focusing on children's learning difficulties

The other four sentences work together to explain why English number naming is systematically confusing, while sentence 3 talks about the human impact of this confusion rather than the linguistic structure itself.

Answer: 3

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. Having an appreciation for the workings of another person's mind is considered a prerequisite for natural language acquisition, strategic social interaction, reflexive thought, and moral judgment.
  2. It is a 'theory of mind' though some scholars prefer to call it 'mentalizing' or 'mindreading', which is important for the development of one's cognitive abilities.
  3. Though we must speculate about its evolutionary origin, we do have indications that the capacity evolved sometime in the last few million years.
  4. This capacity develops from early beginnings in the first year of life to the adult's fast and often effortless understanding of others' thoughts, feelings, and intentions.
  5. One of the most fascinating human capacities is the ability to perceive and interpret other people's behaviour in terms of their mental states.
questions.explanation_text:
Step 1: Find the main topic -> All sentences talk about understanding other people's minds

Step 2: Look for logical flow -> Which sentences connect smoothly?

Let us trace the connection:

  • Sentence 5 introduces the topic: "fascinating human capacity to understand others"
  • Sentence 1 explains why it matters: helps with language, social skills, etc.
  • Sentence 4 shows how it grows: from babies to adults
  • Sentence 3 talks about when it started: evolutionary history

From passage: "It is a 'theory of mind' though some scholars prefer to call it 'mentalizing' or 'mindreading'"

The problem: Sentence 2 starts with "It is..." but what is "it"? The reader gets confused because there's no clear thing being defined right before it.

Flow test: 5 -> 1 -> 4 -> 3 works perfectly!

But inserting 2 anywhere breaks the smooth connection.

Why sentence 2 is the odd one:

🔴 Sentence 2 -> flow-breaker -> Just gives different names for the same thing instead of adding new information. It's like someone interrupting a story to say "Oh, some people call this by different names" which doesn't help the main explanation move forward.

The other four sentences build a complete story: what the capacity is (5) -> why it's important (1) -> how it develops (4) -> where it came from (3).

Sentence 2 only talks about terminology rather than advancing the actual discussion about this mental capacity.

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. What precisely are the "unusual elements" that make a particular case so attractive to a certain kind of audience?
  2. It might be a particularly savage or unfathomable level of depravity, very often it has something to do with the precise amount of mystery involved.
  3. Unsolved, and perhaps unsolvable cases offer something that "ordinary" murder doesn't.
  4. Why are some crimes destined for perpetual re-examination and others locked into permanent obscurity?
questions.explanation_text:
From passage: The sentences discuss crimes that get "perpetual re-examination" versus those in "permanent obscurity" and what makes cases attractive to audiences.

My thought process: Start broad → narrow down → provide answers → elaborate

Sentence 4 asks the big picture question about why some crimes stay famous while others are forgotten → Sentence 1 then asks the specific question about what unusual elements make cases attractive → Sentence 2 answers that question by listing possible elements → Sentence 3 elaborates on one specific type (unsolved cases).

The sequence should be: 4-1-2-3

🟢 4123 is correct → follows perfect logical progression: broad question → specific question → answer → elaboration

This creates smooth flow: "Why do some crimes stay famous?" → "What specific elements attract audiences?" → "It might be depravity or mystery" → "Unsolved cases offer something special"

Each sentence connects naturally to the next, building from general concept to specific details.

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. Algorithms hosted on the internet are accessed by many, so biases in Al models have resulted in much larger impact, adversely affecting far larger groups of people.
  2. Though "algorithmic bias" is the popular term, the foundation of such bias is not in algorithms, but in the data; algorithms are not biased, data is, as algorithms merely reflect persistent patterns that are present in the training data.
  3. Despite their widespread impact, it is relatively easier to fix Al biases than human- generated biases, as it is simpler to identify the former than to try to make people unlearn behaviors learnt over generations.
  4. The impact of biased decisions made by humans is localised and geographically confined, but with the advent of Al, the impact of such decisions is spread over a much wider scale.
questions.explanation_text:
From passage: The sentences discuss the contrast between human bias (localized) and AI bias (widespread), the source of bias (data, not algorithms), and solutions.

Step-by-Step Thought Process:

First, identify the topic -> AI bias and its impact compared to human bias

Next, look for the opening sentence -> Sentence 4 introduces the main contrast (human bias vs AI bias scale)

Then find the building sentence -> Sentence 1 expands on how AI creates larger impact through internet access

Look for explanation sentence -> Sentence 2 clarifies the real source of bias (data, not algorithms)

Finally, find the concluding sentence -> Sentence 3 ends with practical solution perspective

The flow: Problem comparison -> Scale elaboration -> Root cause -> Solution outlook

How to Eliminate Wrong Sequences:

🔴 Starting with 1, 2, or 3 -> scope-error -> These sentences assume you already know the basic contrast. Sentence 4 must come first because it sets up the fundamental comparison between human and AI bias impact.

🔴 Putting 2 before 1 -> context-shift -> You can't explain the source of bias before establishing that AI bias has widespread impact.

🔴 Ending with 1, 2, or 4 -> incomplete-flow -> These don't provide closure. Sentence 3 naturally concludes by offering hope about fixing AI biases.

🟢 Sequence 4123 -> Creates smooth logical progression from problem identification to solution perspective.

The key is recognizing that sentence 4 establishes the foundational contrast that everything else builds upon.

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Colonialism is not a modern phenomenon. World history is full of examples of one society gradually expanding by incorporating adjacent territory and settling its people on newly conquered territory. In the sixteenth century, colonialism changed decisively because of technological developments in navigation that began to connect more remote parts of the world. The modern European colonial project emerged when it became possible to move large numbers of people across the ocean and to maintain political control in spite of geographical dispersion. The term colonialism is used to describe the process of European settlement, violent dispossession and political domination over the rest of the world, including the Americas, Australia, and parts of Africa and Asia.

options.label: A
options.text: Colonialism, conceptualized in the 16th century, allowed colonizers to expand their territories, establish settlements, and exercise political power.

options.label: B
options.text: Colonialism surged in the 16th century due to advancements in navigation, enabling British settlements abroad and global dominance.

options.label: C
options.text: As a result of developments in navigation technology, European colonialism, led to the displacement of indigenous populations and global political changes in the 16th century.

options.label: D
options.text: Technological advancements in navigation in the 16th century, transformed colonialism, enabling Europeans to establish settlements and exert political dominance over distant regions.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what changed about colonialism in the 16th century and why.

From passage: "In the sixteenth century, colonialism changed decisively because of technological developments in navigation that began to connect more remote parts of the world."

The passage says colonialism existed before -> but transformed in the 16th century -> because of navigation technology -> this let Europeans move many people across oceans -> and control distant lands.

Let's check each option for what students often miss:

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> says colonialism was "conceptualized" in 16th century, but passage clearly states it existed before and just changed then. This misses the key point about transformation.

🔴 Option 2 -> too narrow -> says "British" specifically, but passage talks about "European" colonialism generally. Students often pick this because it sounds detailed, but it's actually wrong.

🟠 Option 3 -> partial-truth -> correctly mentions navigation technology and European colonialism, but doesn't capture the crucial idea that colonialism transformed rather than just happened. Misses the "change" aspect.

🟢 Option 4 is correct -> uses "transformed colonialism" which perfectly matches "changed decisively" from the passage. Captures both the technology cause and the European scope accurately.

Key elimination tip: When you see "conceptualized" vs "transformed" - always check if the passage talks about something starting fresh or changing from what existed before!

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Manipulating information was a feature of history long before modern journalism established rules of integrity. A record dates back to ancient Rome, when Antony met Cleopatra and his political enemy Octavian launched a smear campaign against him with "short, sharp slogans written upon coins." The perpetrator became the first Roman Emperor and "fake news had allowed Octavian to hack the republican system once and for all". But the 21st century has seen the weaponization of information on an unprecedented scale. Powerful new technology makes the fabrication of content simple, and social networks amplify falsehoods peddled by States, populist politicians, and dishonest corporate entities. The platforms have become fertile ground for computational propaganda, 'trolling' and 'troll armies'.

options.label: A
options.text: Use of misinformation for attaining power, a practice that is as old as the Octavian era, is currently fueled by technology.

options.label: B
options.text: People need to become critical of what they read, since historically, weaponization of information has led to corruption.

options.label: C
options.text: Disinformation, which is mediated by technology today, is not new and has existed since ancient times.

options.label: D
options.text: Octavian used fake news to manipulate people and attain power and influence, just as people do today.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find the main idea that connects both the historical and modern parts together.

The passage has two key parts: old times (Octavian using fake news for power) and today (technology making fake news much worse). The question is asking what ties these together.

From passage: "fake news had allowed Octavian to hack the republican system" and "21st century has seen the weaponization of information on an unprecedented scale"

My thought process: Historical example of using lies for power -> Modern technology makes this much easier and bigger -> So the main point is that using fake information to get power is old but technology makes it worse now.

Let's check each option by seeing what the passage actually focuses on:

🟢 Option 1 -> correct -> captures both the historical aspect (as old as Octavian) AND the modern technology part, plus mentions the key purpose: attaining power

🔴 Option 2 -> irrelevant -> talks about what people "need to do" but the passage doesn't give advice - it just explains what happens. Also says "corruption" but passage talks about power, not corruption.

🟠 Option 3 -> partial-truth -> correctly says it's old and technology-driven today, but completely misses the main purpose - getting power! The passage emphasizes political power throughout.

🟠 Option 4 -> too narrow -> only focuses on Octavian example but misses the bigger point about how technology makes it much worse today. The passage says modern scale is "unprecedented."

The key insight: Students might get confused between Options 1 and 3 because both mention historical + modern aspects. But Option 3 misses that this is all about political power, which is the main thread connecting Octavian to today's politicians and states.
